body:
The parent issue with description is https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2690 Proposed level changes for requirement in chapter "V6 Cryptography" Full list of requirements for the chapter is listed here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x14-V6-Cryptography.md | # | Description | Level change | | :---: | :--- | :---: | | **6.2.1** | [MODIFIED] Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks. | ~~1 > 2~~
1 > 3 | | **6.2.9** | [ADDED] Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security. | ~~1 > 3~~
1 > 2 | | **6.3.1** | [GRAMMAR, COVERS 6.3.2, LEVEL L2 > L1] Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically-secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition. | 1 > 2 | | **6.3.3** | [GRAMMAR, LEVEL L3 > L1] Verify that random number generation works properly under heavy system load, or that the system degrades gracefully. | 1 > 3 | | **6.5.1** | [ADDED, SPLIT FROM 6.2.2, 6.2.5, COVERS 6.2.3] Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used. | 2 > 1 | | **6.5.4** | [MODIFIED, SPLIT FROM 6.2.2, MOVED FROM 6.2.7] Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm. | 3 > 2 | | **6.6.1** | [ADDED, SPLIT FROM 6.2.2, 6.2.5, COVERS 6.2.3] Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose. | 2 > 1 | | **6.6.3** | [ADDED] Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits. | 1 > 2 | | **6.7.1** | [ADDED] Verify that industry-proven cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This should prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks. | 2 > 3 | | **6.8.2** | [ADDED] Verify that data minimization ensures the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and ensure that data is encrypted immediately after use or as soon as feasible. | 2 > 3 | | **6.9.1** | [ADDED] Verify that a cryptographic inventory is maintained and includes a documented transformation plan or mapping that outlines the migration path from current cryptographic algorithms and systems to those that use post-quantum cryptography. | 2 > 3 | | **6.9.2** | [ADDED] Verify that advancements in the field of post-quantum cryptography are being monitored in order to ensure that the application is aligned with emerging industry standards, and remains prepared for quantum threats. | 2 > 3 | Initially proposed changes, but decided to not make them: | # | Description | Level change | | :---: | :--- | :---: | | **6.2.4** | [MODIFIED, MERGED FROM 1.6.3] Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers or modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This should allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available. | 2 > 3 |

comments.body:
6.2.1 is such a difficult attack to weaponize and it's only valid on legacy encryption that is no longer recommended. I suggesting leaving it at 2, 3 or even remove it.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **6.2.1** | [MODIFIED] Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks. | 1 > 2 |

6.2.4 is so critical for the post quantum world, which is coming up faster than expected due to recent innovations, that I suggest leaving it as 2.

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **6.2.4** | [MODIFIED, MERGED FROM 1.6.3] Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers or modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This should allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available. | 2 > 3 |

6.2.9 is pretty basic and fundamental to good security. Maybe leave it at 2?

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **6.2.9** | [ADDED] Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security. | 1 > 3 |

Moving 6.2.9 to L3 seems too much. I don't this we can say that using correct crypto is required only for super-secure apps. L2 should be fine. At the same time, this requirement seems to complement 6.6.1 which is moved to L1.

For 6.7.1, I think L3 is too much as well. This requirement covers using decent TLS parameters (ciphersuites, etc.) and make sure than "adversary-in-the-middle attacks" is prevented. I think this is a standard/basic security requirement (L2).

> Moving 6.2.9 to L3 seems too much. I don't this we can say that using correct crypto is required only for super-secure apps. L2 should be fine. At the say time, this requirement seems to complement 6.6.1 which is moved to L1.
> 
> For 6.7.1, I think L3 is too much as well. This requirement covers using decent TLS parameters (ciphersuites, etc.) and make sure than "adversary-in-the-middle attacks" is prevented. I think this is a standard/basic security requirement (L2).
> 

I agree with both of these.

My thoughts:

* Based on @jmanico's thoughts, I think maybe 6.2.1 is niche and should therefore be L3.
* 6.2.4 crypto agility is really hard but based on @jmanico's thoughts and also thinking about it it more, I think it is a really important but undervalued topic, especially with the quantum issue. I would agree with dropping to L2.
* For 6.2.9 I am prepared to accept that L3 is too high and this does seem like a relatively basic key length requirement.
* For 6.7.1, how often do we think that developers are rolling their own key exchange process? I think we cover the TLS aspects in V9 so this particular requirement therefore seems a little niche. What do you think @jmanico @randomstuff  ?

If my mind, 6.7.1 is just a small configuration change in TLS and is never something I use outside of TLS. It's really easy to get this right. Because of the ease, I think L2 is sensible. 

But I would even vote to drop 6.7.1 and just roll it into a high level requirement that says "configure your TLS based on industry best practices" and roll up many of the TLS requirements into one larger TLS requirement.

And last, I think the crypto work is excellent and merits a new C-ASVS just on crypto someday. Even if we do roll-up many of these requirements I would hate to lose them.

> If my mind, 6.7.1 is just a small configuration change in TLS and is never something I use outside of TLS. It's really easy to get this right. Because of the ease, I think L2 is sensible.

I agree that it is not something that we would expect to happen much outside of TLS (and DTLS and SRTP when using WebRTC) in regular applications.

Other scenarios would be:

* a Github/Gitlab-style application providing git repo access over SSH;
* an integrated bastion solution or a VM manager solution providing access the machines through a web interface and through a SSH interface;

if that is considered in scope.

> But I would even vote to drop 6.7.1 and just roll it into a high level requirement that says "configure your TLS based on industry best practices" and roll up many of the TLS requirements into one larger TLS requirement.

Yes that may be an option.

I think we already have TLS related requirements in V9 so I think we are covered for TLS use cases.

The other usecases you mentioned above are clearly a lot more niche hence the L3 suggestion.
Agree with most of these, will be sorting a PR based on it today
ping @danielcuthbert - probably it is easier to head your feedback / agreements / disagreements on the discussed requirement levels and we (me or Josh) handle the PR part.
@danielcuthbert I have opened #2764 for now as we are at crunch time :) If you can take a look on Monday that would be great, otherwise we will merge in so we can keep moving :)
I prefer we merge in, and if there is a reason for changes, we can make them later.

Summary of discussed requirements:
* 6.2.1 - initially proposed 1 > 2, changed to 1 > 3
* 6.2.4 - initially proposed 2 > 3, stays at L2
* 6.2.9 - initially proposed 1 > 3, changed to 1 > 2
* 6.7.1 - initially proposed 2 > 3, made 2 > 3

I'll merge those in. If there is a need to change them, please open a separate issue to handle it.

Fair one, @danielcuthbert we have big changes happening this week in preparation for RC1 so we didn't want to leave dangling changes open. If you want to continue discussion on this issue or PR #2764 then please let me know.
